university: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence Policy (AI-001)
documents.summary: UTRGV's AI-001 is an institution-wide governance policy for developing, buying and deploying AI systems, with principles, risk assessment, inventory and training duties. It says almost nothing about student use of AI in coursework or academic integrity.
documents.stance_why: The policy sets no rule on whether students may use AI in courses. Its only conduct rule is a ban on "Discriminatory, biased, malicious, or harmful use of AI" and a duty to follow existing law. Course-level decisions are not addressed, and it points to "individual division or college AI policies". I coded delegates because it hands the matter to other bodies by silence rather than setting a stance.

units.why: The purpose statement sets the institution-wide purpose of the policy: "guidelines and ethical standards for the development, deployment, and utilization of AI technologies". That is a framework preamble, so P56, general phase, informs.
units.anchor: establish guidelines and ethical standards for the development, deployment, and utilization of AI technologies

units.why: States the values the university balances in AI use ("protecting privacy, fairness, security, and academic integrity"); a principles preamble, so P56.
units.anchor: UTRGV fosters innovation while protecting privacy, fairness, security, and academic integrity.

units.why: Lists the named principles the university adopts for AI; this is the institution-level principles framework (P56), not a rule on a specific use.
units.anchor: adopts principles of fairness, transparency, accountability, human oversight, privacy-by-design, security-by-design, and continuous improvement

units.why: Scope statement: the policy binds "faculty, staff, students, contractors, and vendors" who design, procure, configure or deploy AI. It sets what the policy covers (P61 definitions and scope). It targets deployers, not ordinary student users.
units.anchor: applies to faculty, staff, students, contractors, and vendors who design, procure, configure, or deploy AI

units.why: A definition of AI that fixes the term used in the policy: "simulation of human intelligence processes by machines". P61.
units.anchor: Artificial Intelligence (AI) refers to the simulation of human intelligence processes by machines

units.why: Defines generative AI ("create new content, such as text, images, or music"), setting what the policy covers; P61.
units.anchor: A type of AI that can create new content, such as text, images, or music

units.why: Defines personal data, tying it to compliance with Texas privacy law for AI systems. A definition that scopes privacy duties, so P61 with a fit note that it defines data rather than AI.
units.anchor: any information that is linked or reasonably linkable to an identified or identifiable individual
units.fit_note: Defines personal data and ties it to TDPSA and TRAIGA compliance rather than defining AI itself.

units.why: Names the officer and committee that own the AI policy ("AI Risk Officer (AIRO)", "AI Governance Committee"): P80.
units.anchor: UTRGV designates AI Risk Officer (AIRO) and establishes an AI Governance Committee

units.why: Assigns duties to the AIRO (inventory, risk classification, monitoring, incident reporting). Who implements and monitors the policy is P80.
units.anchor: The AIRO ensures that an AI Inventory is established and maintained, classifies risk, coordinates assessments

units.why: Describes what the committee does ("sets standards, reviews heightened-risk deployments"); assigns policy ownership and oversight, P80.
units.anchor: The AI Governance Committee sets standards, reviews heightened‑risk deployments, approves assessment instruments

units.why: Clarifies the committee's relation to existing governance ("does not replace existing governance structures"); a statement on who owns the policy, so P80.
units.anchor: does not replace existing governance structures

units.why: Places responsibility on university units for ethical and compliant AI use. Closest type is P80 (who owns/enforces), but it is a duty for every unit rather than naming an office.
units.anchor: Units remain responsible for the ethical and compliant use of AI within their operations.
units.fit_note: Assigns responsibility to every unit for ethical and compliant use, not naming a single owning office.

units.why: Binds all users to existing law and university policy for AI use ("abiding by all established laws, rules, regulations, policies"): P77.
units.anchor: Users are responsible for abiding by all established laws, rules, regulations, policies, and other university

units.why: A flat ban on "discriminatory, biased, malicious, or harmful use of AI" for all users. A general conduct rule, so P74 and unit_stance prohibit.
units.anchor: Discriminatory, biased, malicious, or harmful use of AI is strictly prohibited.

units.why: Requires ethical review of AI development and AI-driven automated decision making by the data owner. It is institutional review of AI systems, so P65.
units.anchor: must undergo an ethical review by the data owner

units.why: Requires handling of personal and confidential data under law and policy in AI applications; protecting personal data is P50.
units.anchor: handle personal, sensitive, and confidential data in accordance with relevant laws, regulations, and University policies

units.why: Tells users to follow IP and copyright law for AI technologies (software, models, datasets); P52 covers copyright and ownership.
units.anchor: follow all UTRGV and UT System guidance and all applicable intellectual property and copyright laws

units.why: Bans unauthorized distribution, copying or modification of AI-related resources, an IP rule on AI software and models (P52).
units.anchor: Unauthorized distribution, copying, or modification of AI-related resources is prohibited.

units.why: Requires transparency and defined responsibility for AI system outcomes. This is accountability for deployed systems; nearest is P80 (who is responsible), noted as partial.
units.anchor: The development and use of AI systems must be transparent, and the responsibility for AI
units.fit_note: Requires transparency and clearly defined responsibility for AI system outcomes, not naming an owner of the policy.

units.why: Requires notices and bars presenting AI as human ("do not misrepresent AI as human"). People must be told when they interact with AI: P103.
units.anchor: do not misrepresent AI as human

units.why: Requires labelling synthetic media and provenance measures for generative output. Closest is P103 (telling people they face AI content), but it is about labelling output.
units.anchor: Label synthetic media and use content provenance measures
units.fit_note: Labelling of synthetic media and provenance metadata on generated outputs, not only notice of interacting with an AI system.

units.why: Requires model cards for public-facing AI systems; documenting deployed AI systems is P98.
units.anchor: Maintain system/model cards for applicable public‑facing systems.

units.why: Requires complaint and redress channels for AI systems. A reporting channel for AI problems fits P71 partly; it is a channel for those affected rather than a duty to report.
units.anchor: Offer complaint and redress channels with published response expectations.
units.fit_note: Complaint and redress channel for people affected by AI systems, not a duty to report incidents.

units.why: Requires security measures for AI systems (credentials, patches). A security-practice duty not covered by a type about phishing or data privacy, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Users must take measures to ensure the security of AI systems
units.uncovered_note: Users must secure AI systems (protect credentials, apply patches, follow security requirements).

units.why: Requires bias testing of AI models; ethical and bias concerns are P53.
units.anchor: AI algorithms and models must be designed and tested to minimize bias and discrimination.

units.why: Says involvement of stakeholder groups, including students, is "essential" (and participation is "encouraged"). Engaging the community: P88 as nearest.
units.anchor: the involvement of relevant stakeholder groups is essential
units.fit_note: Stakeholder involvement of students, faculty and affected parties in AI projects, not partnerships or forums.

units.why: The university encourages AI education and research. It is a stated institutional stance favoring AI, the closest being P02 (encourage AI), though it does not set a rule for coursework.
units.anchor: UTRGV encourages education and research in AI and related fields.
units.fit_note: Encourages AI education and research at the institutional level, not a default for student coursework.

units.why: Asks users to work to eliminate bias; bias and fairness concerns are P53.
units.anchor: Users should strive to eliminate bias from AI systems and promote fairness in their applications.

units.why: Users must verify AI-generated content ("independently verified for accuracy and reliability"): P31.
units.anchor: any AI-generated content they choose to use has been independently verified for accuracy and reliability

units.why: Users stay accountable for decisions facilitated by AI. Closest is P29 (students own what they submit), applied to all users.
units.anchor: Individuals using AI technologies are accountable for their actions and decisions facilitated by AI systems.
units.fit_note: Applies to all users' actions and decisions, not specifically to submitted student work.

units.why: Forbids sole reliance on AI for important choices, so a human stays responsible for consequential decisions: P73.
units.anchor: Do not solely rely on AI recommendations when making important choices.

units.why: Requires lawful, consented data collection for AI applications; a privacy and data rule (P50).
units.anchor: Data used in AI applications must be collected in accordance with existing UTRGV and UT

units.why: Accessibility of AI systems for people with disabilities: P97.
units.anchor: AI applications and systems should be designed to be accessible to all, including individuals with

units.why: The Prohibited Activities section only bans conduct that violates existing policy or law; compliance with existing rules is P77.
units.anchor: Users must refrain from engaging in any conduct that violates UTRGV, UT System, State of

units.why: Limits confidential data to AI tools evaluated by IT and ISO ("approved AI tools"): vetted-tool and data protection, P50.
units.anchor: Controlled and confidential data may only be used with approved AI tools that have been

units.why: Says all AI tools, even for public data, must pass IT and ISO assessment: review and approval of AI tools, P65.
units.anchor: all AI tools must undergo and pass the necessary IT and ISO technology assessment processes

units.why: Requires an AI Risk Assessment before deployment and after changes; institutional review of AI systems (P65).
units.anchor: complete an AI Risk Assessment

units.why: Requires an impact assessment for AI systems; review of AI systems before deployment, P65.
units.anchor: Complete an AI Impact Assessment addressing stakeholders

units.why: Requires a human oversight plan with authority to override for consequential AI uses; humans stay responsible for consequential decisions (P73).
units.anchor: Provide a Human Oversight Plan for consequential uses

units.why: Requires committee approval and AIRO sign-off before deploying AI: approval of AI systems, P65.
units.anchor: Obtain approval from the AI Governance Committee and AIRO sign‑off prior to deployment.

units.why: Requires evaluation plans for deployed AI; testing and monitoring of AI systems, P98.
units.anchor: Define and execute evaluation plans covering accuracy, robustness, fairness, toxicity, and privacy leakage

units.why: Requires adversarial testing and documented mitigations for AI systems: audit and monitoring of deployed systems, P98.
units.anchor: Conduct adversarial testing for prompt injection, jailbreaks, model extraction, data poisoning, and privacy leakage

units.why: Requires ongoing monitoring of deployed AI with rollback triggers: P98.
units.anchor: Monitor production Key Performance Indicators

units.why: Sets incident response for AI: notification and post-incident review. Reporting AI incidents, P71.
units.anchor: Maintain incident taxonomy and contact matrix; notify regulators/partners as applicable

units.why: Sets a semiannual reassessment cycle for higher-risk AI systems; monitoring over time, P98.
units.anchor: Reassess heightened‑risk systems at least semiannually and after material changes

units.why: Requires registration of all AI systems in an inventory before pilot or deployment; documenting AI systems, P98.
units.anchor: All AI systems must be registered in the AI Inventory

units.why: Requires AI use to comply with federal, state, UT System and UTRGV rules: P77.
units.anchor: AI use at UTRGV must comply with relevant Federal laws, State of Texas regulations, UT

units.why: Requires GDPR compliance for AI systems: compliance with existing law (P77).
units.anchor: AI systems must comply with GDPR requirements regarding data protection and privacy.

units.why: Mandates annual AI training for non-student account holders ("must complete AI training ... annually"); AI training is P70. Students are explicitly excluded.
units.anchor: must complete AI training provided by the Information Security Office annually

units.why: Requires technology assessment of any product with AI before purchase: P65.
units.anchor: must undergo a Technology Assessment through UTRGV approved workflows before purchase

units.why: Sets procurement contract requirements for AI vendors (NIST alignment, audit rights): review of AI vendors, P65.
units.anchor: Contracts must require alignment with NIST AI RMF, transparency documentation

units.why: Requires periodic re-evaluation of higher-risk vendor AI: P65 (broadened to periodic re-evaluation).
units.anchor: Ensure periodic reassessment for heightened‑risk vendor systems.

units.why: States a consequence for violating the policy ("suspension of system access or use"); concrete penalties, P37, though generic and not specific to student coursework.
units.anchor: Non‑compliance may result in suspension of system access or use
units.fit_note: Generic consequence (suspension of access) for non-compliance, not a graded-work penalty.

units.why: Annual review cycle for the policy; P54.
units.anchor: This policy will be reviewed at least annually or upon significant regulatory or technological change.

documents.unit: Center for Online Learning and Teaching Technology (COLTT)
documents.title: Generative AI Technology
documents.summary: COLTT's page gives faculty background, strategies and assessment ideas for generative AI. It tells instructors to set clear syllabus policies and says detectors must not be the sole basis for misconduct findings.
documents.stance_why: The page tells instructors to "Clearly outline expectations regarding the use of Generative AI tools" and to state "Whether AI use is permitted or restricted", leaving the decision to each course. It sets no university stance, so delegates.

units.why: Says the page "will continue to be updated with new guidance", i.e. the guidance is provisional and revisited: P54.
units.anchor: will continue to be updated with new guidance, resources, and recommended readings as they become

units.why: Defines generative AI for faculty readers, setting what the guidance covers: P61.
units.anchor: Generative AI refers to a category of Artificial Intelligence systems designed to create new content

units.why: Says AI tools can serve instruction and productivity "when used thoughtfully and in alignment with course expectations". It names benefits of AI for teaching, with conditions: P87.
units.anchor: when used thoughtfully and in alignment with course expectations and institutional guidelines

units.why: Warns outputs can be wrong or biased and says to verify AI information before academic use: P31.
units.anchor: it is important to verify AI-generated information before using it in academic or professional work

units.why: One of the listed 'potential misuse' concerns: AI "completing programming assignments". It frames AI doing graded work as misuse, which is P19, though only as a concern, not a rule.
units.anchor: Completing programming assignments
units.policy: AI completing programming assignments is named as a potential misuse of generative AI.
units.fit_note: Framed as a concern within the educational community, not as a rule students must follow.

units.why: Listed as a potential misuse ("Generating student essays, papers, or creative work"); AI producing submitted work, P19, as a concern only.
units.anchor: Generating student essays, papers, or creative work
units.policy: Generating student essays, papers, or creative work with AI is named as a potential misuse.
units.fit_note: Framed as a concern, not a rule.

units.why: Listed as a potential misuse: AI "answering quiz or exam questions". Nearest is P22 (no AI on exams), though stated only as a concern.
units.anchor: Answering quiz or exam questions
units.policy: Using AI to answer quiz or exam questions is named as a potential misuse.
units.fit_note: Framed as a concern about misuse, not a prohibition on exams.

units.why: Says AI output should be critically evaluated; P31.
units.anchor: All AI-generated output should be evaluated critically.

units.why: Frames AI-related integrity worries as continuous with older issues. It sets no rule and fits no type, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: concerns related to academic integrity predate Generative AI
units.uncovered_note: Says similar tools and integrity concerns predate generative AI, normalizing AI as a continuation of existing issues.

units.why: Tells instructors to learn the tools first ("becoming familiar with Generative AI tools", "try using these tools yourself"): P63 on faculty learning before setting policy.
units.anchor: A critical first step is becoming familiar with Generative AI tools

units.why: Tells instructors to state AI expectations in the syllabus ("Syllabus: Set Clear Policies"). P09.
units.anchor: Clearly outline expectations regarding the use of Generative AI tools in your course.

units.why: First of three listed elements instructors should state: "Whether AI use is permitted or restricted". It leaves the stance to each instructor, so P04.
units.anchor: Whether AI use is permitted or restricted
units.policy: The syllabus should state whether AI use is permitted or restricted.

units.why: Second element: the syllabus should state "expectations for citation or acknowledgment" of AI. The instructor sets disclosure expectations; nearest P24.
units.anchor: Expectations for citation or acknowledgment
units.policy: The syllabus should state expectations for citation or acknowledgment of AI use.
units.fit_note: Tells instructors to state a disclosure expectation rather than requiring disclosure from all students.

units.why: Third element: the syllabus should state "consequences for inappropriate use". Penalties stated in advance, P37.
units.anchor: Consequences for inappropriate use
units.policy: The syllabus should state consequences for inappropriate AI use.

units.why: Course AI policies should follow "course learning outcomes": P83.
units.anchor: Policies should align with course learning outcomes and institutional guidance.

units.why: Tells instructors to discuss AI with students, covering capabilities, limitations, ethics and relevance: P66.
units.anchor: having open conversations with students about Generative AI

units.why: Asks instructors to tell students critical thinking and digital literacy matter for work. The career argument is about skills: P44, with a fit note.
units.anchor: critical thinking, evaluation of information, and digital literacy are essential skills that extend beyond the
units.fit_note: Frames critical thinking and digital literacy, not AI use itself, as workforce skills.

units.why: Encourages instructors to ask students to acknowledge AI use "when appropriate": P24, optional and instructor-determined.
units.anchor: asking students to acknowledge AI use when appropriate

units.why: Gives the reason that "AI shortcuts" limit skill development, part of the "Growth Mindset" advice: P41.
units.anchor: Too much reliance on AI shortcuts can limit opportunities to develop essential skills

units.why: Suggests lower-stakes exams to "reduce pressure and discourage misuse". It redesigns grading around AI: P35. It differs from P33, which shifts weight to proctored work.
units.anchor: consider avoiding high-stakes weighting

units.why: Suggests exam time limits (30 seconds per true/false question, etc.) to limit outside search. An assessment redesign: P35.
units.anchor: Appropriate time limits can reduce opportunities to search for answers externally.

units.why: Suggests lockdown browsers with monitoring to deter misconduct on online exams. Closed-device exam rules are P22; this is a tool suggestion, so P22 with a note.
units.anchor: Tools such as Lockdown browsers with monitoring features may help deter misconduct.
units.fit_note: Suggests proctoring tools to deter misconduct but does not ban AI on exams.

units.why: Says detectors "are not definitive" and must never be the "sole basis" for misconduct decisions. It is the evidence-standard rule (P69) rather than declining to use detectors (P39).
units.anchor: should never be used as the sole basis for academic misconduct decisions

units.why: Keeps human judgment and institutional policy in misconduct decisions; P73 (humans decide on people), applied to misconduct.
units.anchor: Human judgment and institutional policies remain essential.

units.why: Recommends Turnitin to support integrity; similarity checks to identify misuse, P40.
units.anchor: Use a plagiarism detection tool such as Turnitin to support academic integrity.

units.why: Warns that similarity scores do not equal plagiarism, so reports must be read carefully: evidence standards (P69).
units.anchor: similarity percentages may include properly cited sources and reference lists and do not automatically indicate

units.why: Says Turnitin's AI writing results "are not always accurate" and not the "sole basis" for decisions: evidence standard for detector output, P69.
units.anchor: these results are not always accurate and should not be used as the sole basis

units.why: Final misconduct determinations rest on human judgment and academic policy: P73.
units.anchor: Human judgment and institutional academic policies must guide any final determinations.

units.why: Suggests clear rubrics to deter misuse. This redesigns grading around AI, so P35.
units.anchor: Using clear rubrics with well-defined criteria can help deter inappropriate AI use

units.why: Advises assignments linking content to personal experience, "more difficult for AI tools to replicate": P35.
units.anchor: Design assignments that require students to connect course content to personal experiences

units.why: Says instructors may build AI into activities because students will meet AI at work: P79 (AI built into coursework), with the workplace reason noted.
units.anchor: instructors may consider designing activities that intentionally incorporate AI use

units.why: Gives the workplace reason for including AI in assessment: P44, learning to use AI as a professional skill.
units.anchor: Since students are likely to encounter AI tools in the workplace

units.why: First of the listed uses of AI in education: "formative feedback on writing". Writing support, P91.
units.anchor: Providing formative feedback on writing
units.policy: Generative AI can provide formative feedback on writing.

units.why: Lists AI as "a supplemental FAQ or study aid": study aids, P14.
units.anchor: Serving as a supplemental FAQ or study aid
units.policy: Generative AI can serve as a supplemental FAQ or study aid.

units.why: Lists AI generation of "summaries, flashcards, or practice questions": P14.
units.anchor: Generating summaries, flashcards, or practice questions
units.policy: Generative AI can generate summaries, flashcards, or practice questions.

units.why: Lists "tutoring and step-by-step explanations" as uses: AI as a tutor, P12.
units.anchor: Assisting with tutoring and step-by-step explanations
units.policy: Generative AI can assist with tutoring and step-by-step explanations.

units.why: Lists language learning and translation as uses; writing support, P91 with a note on translation.
units.anchor: Supporting language learning and translation
units.policy: Generative AI can support language learning and translation.
units.fit_note: Covers language learning and translation more than editing and proofreading.

units.why: Lists AI help creating "instructional materials or assessments", an instructor use in teaching work: P59.
units.anchor: Helping create instructional materials or assessments
units.policy: Generative AI can help create instructional materials or assessments.

units.why: Lists accessibility support (alternative formats, summaries) as an AI use: P97.
units.anchor: Supporting accessibility through alternative formats and summaries
units.policy: Generative AI can support accessibility through alternative formats and summaries.

units.why: Says AI "should not replace instructors" but assist them. An instructor-use boundary on teaching work, P59.
units.anchor: Generative AI should not replace instructors, but rather assist educators

documents.title: Learner-Centered Syllabus Design (generative AI syllabus statements)
tiers: Exploratory use (AI embedded in course activities)
Permitted use as specified by the instructor

documents.stance_why: The page offers three model statements and calls them "only an example and optional", with "Please modify as you see fit". Because it offers tiers or templates for instructors to pick, the stance is delegates.

units.why: The statements are "only an example and optional": the CTE does not set a university rule and leaves syllabus choices to instructors. P04.
units.anchor: These potential approaches are only an example and optional in case you would like to

units.why: Instructors may adapt the statements to their values and "course learning objectives"; decision per instructor (P04), tied to objectives (P83). I chose P04 because the main message is instructor discretion.
units.anchor: Please modify as you see fit and align to your teaching values, beliefs, and course

units.why: Offers three named options (exploratory, permitted, no use); a menu of tiers, P05.
units.anchor: Use of Generative AI as Exploratory Potential
units.policy: The CTE offers three suggested syllabus approaches to generative AI: exploratory, permitted as specified by the instructor, and no use.

units.why: Statement 1 sample text: the instructor "intend[s] to embed" AI in the course. It builds AI into coursework: P79.
units.anchor: I intend to embed the use of them in my course

units.why: Sample wording says AI use is for specific activities tied to "course learning objectives". P83.
units.anchor: We will use AI tools for specific activities and assignments as aligned to course learning

units.why: Statement 2 sample text: AI used "throughout the semester for specific activities and assignments". Permission as specified by the instructor: P04.
units.anchor: We will use AI tools throughout the semester for specific activities and assignments

units.why: Statement 2 sends students to syllabus sections and assignments for the AI rules: P78.
units.anchor: please consult the appropriate sections of this syllabus or individual assignments that reference targeted AI

units.why: Sample wording invites students to contact the instructor with questions about AI use: P10.
units.anchor: If you have questions about how your use of generative AI technologies align with our

units.why: Statement 3 sample text bans "generative AI in any form" in the course: P01.
units.anchor: The use of generative AI in any form is strictly prohibited in this course.

units.why: Sample no-use wording bans creating "essays, creative works, code, or solutions for assignments or exams" with AI: P19 for submitted work.
units.anchor: Students are not permitted to employ generative AI tools, algorithms, or models to create any

units.why: Sample wording: chatbot misuse gets "the same penalties as plagiarism", classifying it as plagiarism: P36.
units.anchor: Using chatbots in this manner will incur the same penalties as plagiarism

units.why: Sample no-use wording says building skills prepares students for success; the reason is skill building: P41.
units.anchor: Developing strong competencies in the skills associated with this course

units.why: Sample statement grounds the rule in academic integrity: P95.
units.anchor: I firmly uphold the principles of academic integrity and the ethical pursuit of knowledge.

notes: No computing or school-level unit found. AI-001 mostly governs system development and procurement, so most units are P65/P98/P80/P77; few student-facing rules. P65 and P98 are used broadly for system review and monitoring. Syllabus page: the three model statements are optional templates, so sample-wording units describe what the template says rather than a binding rule. Several fit_notes mark loose fits (P80, P103, P88).
